Conceptual Design of an AI-Powered Driver Assistance System Prototype
Saarthi Copilot v1: System Architecture, Hardware, Software and AI Design
Week 3: Conceptual Design of an AI-Powered Driver Assistance System Prototype

This document presents the conceptual design of Saarthi Copilot v1, a prototype AI-powered driver assistance system that improves vehicle safety by warning drivers about drowsiness, distraction, forward collision risk, unsafe following distance, lane departure and overspeeding, and by flagging vehicle faults before they cause breakdowns. It turns the product concept from the Week 1 roadmap into a buildable design and applies the Week 2 feasibility findings by starting with an affordable camera-based configuration that can later grow into a full camera–radar–LiDAR fusion system.

The prototype is a windscreen-mounted unit with a forward HDR camera, an infrared driver-facing camera, an edge AI processor and a read-only connection to the vehicle's OBD-II port, with an optional 77 GHz radar for commercial fleets. All perception runs on the device. Eleven software modules handle sensor acquisition, forward perception, driver monitoring, vehicle health, tracking and time-to-collision, context, risk assessment, driver interaction, event recording and system health. A hybrid decision engine combines explainable rule-based thresholds with a learned risk score and makes collision warnings earlier when the driver is drowsy. Alerts escalate through four levels using short voice messages in Hindi and English. The design targets an end-to-end warning latency of about 90 ms, fewer than one false alert per driving hour and a production bill of materials of about ₹7,500. The document also covers the justification for each AI algorithm, hardware and software choices, safety, security and privacy, limitations, future scalability and a build-and-validation plan.

The Week 1 roadmap defined Saarthi Copilot as an edge-AI co-pilot for Indian roads and planned 20 prototype units by Month 9. The Week 2 study concluded that AI-based sensor fusion is feasible now for driver assistance and recommended a tiered approach, starting with lower-cost sensor sets. This document is the bridge between those strategy documents and engineering work: it defines what the prototype must do, how it is built, how data moves through it, and why each technical choice was made.

Version 1 is a warning-only system: it informs the driver but never steers, brakes or accelerates. Such warning features are classed as Level 0 (no driving automation) under SAE J3016, which keeps the safety case manageable for a first product. The prototype is designed for passenger cars, light commercial vehicles, buses and trucks fitted with a standard OBD port, as provided by modern vehicles built to BS-VI emission norms.

3.2 How AI Has Changed Driver Assistance

Early driver assistance relied on radar with hand-tuned rules. First-generation camera systems used classical computer vision: boosted cascades in the style of Viola and Jones for faces and vehicles, histogram-of-oriented-gradients features with support vector machines for pedestrians, and Hough transforms for straight lane lines. These methods worked on clean highways but struggled with changing light, clutter and unusual objects. Deep convolutional networks, which leapt ahead in image recognition from 2012, changed this: one-stage detectors such as YOLO made accurate, real-time detection possible on embedded hardware, and newer transformer and bird's-eye-view models now fuse several cameras and sensors.

Driver monitoring followed a similar path, moving from indirect cues such as steering-wheel movement to infrared cameras that track the eyes, head and gaze directly. Regulation has followed: the EU General Safety Regulation requires drowsiness and attention warning, and later advanced distraction warning, in new vehicles, and Euro NCAP rewards effective driver monitoring. AI is therefore no longer an optional extra; it is the core of modern driver assistance.

A truck driver is on the Indore–Bhopal highway at 2 a.m., ten hours into a shift. Saarthi Copilot notices that the driver's eyes are closing more often and for longer, and that the truck is drifting within its lane. It plays a soft chime and says in Hindi, "You seem tired. Please take a break soon." At the same time, the decision engine starts giving collision warnings earlier than usual, because a drowsy driver reacts more slowly. Ten minutes later the driver's eyes stay closed for over a second while the truck drifts towards the road edge. The device immediately issues a loud voice warning. When this happens again, it escalates to the critical level and notifies the fleet manager, who calls the driver to arrange a rest stop. A short clip of each event is saved and later uploaded for coaching, without any continuous video ever leaving the truck.

The prototype uses a developer-friendly edge AI module with mature tools, which speeds up model development and debugging. The production version moves to an automotive-grade SoC of around 8 TOPS, which is cheaper, uses less power and is qualified for wider temperatures. Keeping the software modular, with a hardware abstraction layer between the application and the inference runtime, makes this port practical. Heat is the hardest hardware problem in a windscreen device under the Indian sun. The unit is mounted in the shaded area behind the rear-view mirror, uses an aluminium heat spreader coupled to the mounting bracket, and pulses the IR LEDs only during camera exposure. If the processor approaches its thermal limit, a graceful-degradation policy first lowers the forward camera frame rate from 30 to 15 fps and pauses non-safety features such as sign recognition and high-quality recording, while keeping driver monitoring and collision warning active.

Every algorithm was chosen against five criteria: (1) accuracy on Indian road and driver data; (2) speed on edge hardware within the latency budget; (3) explainability, so that alerts can be justified and tested; (4) robustness to lighting, weather and driver variety; and (5) the ability to improve over time through OTA updates. Where a simpler, explainable method meets the need, it is preferred over a more complex one.

Object detection uses a small one-stage convolutional detector from the YOLO family, quantised to INT8. Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN are more accurate on small objects but too slow for the target hardware, and transformer detectors are still heavy for low-power processors. The detector is pre-trained on large public datasets and fine-tuned on the India Driving Dataset and pilot data, with classes including car, bus, truck, auto-rickshaw, motorcycle, bicycle, pedestrian and animal.

Distance is estimated from a single camera using ground-plane geometry. For a camera at height H above the road with focal length f (in pixels), an object whose base appears y_b pixels in the image, with the horizon at row y_h, is at distance:

This is refined with typical real-world sizes for each object class and, when fitted, replaced by radar measurements. Stereo cameras or LiDAR would be more accurate but would break the cost target, so they are left to later tiers, as recommended in Week 2.

Lanes are detected with a row-anchor lane detection network in the style of Ultra Fast Lane Detection, which is extremely fast because it predicts lane positions row by row instead of classifying every pixel. Because many Indian roads have no markings, a lightweight drivable-area segmentation head on the same backbone finds road edges, so lane departure warnings still work on unmarked roads. Traffic signs are found by the main detector and classified by a small MobileNet-style classifier, pre-trained on public sign datasets such as GTSRB and fine-tuned on Indian signs.

Objects are tracked with a Kalman filter and Hungarian-algorithm matching, the approach used by SORT and extended by ByteTrack to keep low-confidence detections. This is far cheaper than deep appearance-based trackers and provides the relative speed needed for collision risk. Time-to-collision is computed from distance d and closing speed v_rel, and cross-checked with the rate at which an object's image grows, which does not depend on distance estimates:
TTC ≈ Δt / (s − 1),     where s = w(t) / w(t − Δt)     (3)
Here w is the object's width in the image and Δt the time between frames. Headway is the time gap to the vehicle ahead at the current speed:

A lightweight face detector of the BlazeFace class finds the face in each infrared frame, and a landmark network locates points around the eyes, mouth and nose. Eye openness is measured with the eye aspect ratio (EAR), which uses six landmarks p1–p6 around each eye:
From EAR the system computes PERCLOS, the percentage of time the eyes are at least 80% closed over a rolling window T, which is one of the best-validated measures of drowsiness:
PERCLOS = ( time with eyes ≥ 80% closed during T ) / T × 100%     (6)

Head pose is estimated by fitting the landmarks to a 3D face model, and a gaze network estimates where the driver is looking, so eyes-off-road time can be measured as distraction regulations expect. A small object detector spots a phone near the face or hands. These features, together with blink duration, yawn frequency, head nods, lane weaving from M3 and time on task, feed a temporal classifier (a small recurrent network or gradient-boosted model) that outputs a drowsiness score from 0 to 1. Training labels come from the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS), a standard self-rating of sleepiness. Combining several validated measures is more reliable than a single PERCLOS threshold and, unlike an end-to-end video network, it can explain why an alert was raised.

Labelled examples of vehicle failures are rare, so a supervised classifier is impractical. Instead, an autoencoder learns what normal OBD signal patterns look like for each vehicle, and an Isolation Forest flags unusual combinations, such as rising coolant temperature at normal load or falling battery voltage during cranking. These are combined with standard fault-code (DTC) rules to produce maintenance alerts.

The decision engine is deliberately hybrid. A rule-based state machine, with thresholds for TTC, headway, lane offset and eyes-off-road time, makes every alert predictable and testable. A gradient-boosted risk model, trained on pilot data, adjusts alert timing based on context such as speed, road type and traffic density. The most important adaptation is driver-state-aware timing: the collision warning threshold grows as the drowsiness score D rises, giving a tired driver more time to react:
TTC_warn = TTC_base + k · D,     e.g. TTC_base = 2.5 s, k = 1.0 s, D ∈ [0, 1]     (7)

All networks use quantisation-aware training to run in INT8 with minimal accuracy loss, are pruned where possible, and are compiled with the target's inference engine. Detection, lanes and drivable area share one backbone, so the forward camera needs a single main network pass per frame.

Figure 4 shows the escalation logic. Alerts move up through four levels as risk grows or the driver fails to respond, and move back down when the driver responds and the risk clears. Sudden hazards, such as a vehicle cutting in, skip directly to the warning level.

Lane departure warnings are suppressed below 30 km/h and during deliberate lane changes. Where the turn indicator signal is available (OEM integration or decoded CAN data), it is used directly; otherwise deliberate changes are inferred from smooth lateral motion and yaw rate.

Drivers can choose the language and say "Saarthi, repeat" to hear the last message again. Safety alerts cannot be switched off by voice.
9. End-to-End Workflow: Data Acquisition, Processing and Response
The complete workflow, from ignition to a cloud report, runs as follows:
Start-up: on ignition, the device boots, runs self-tests, checks camera calibration and is ready within 15 seconds.
Acquisition: cameras stream at 30 fps, OBD data is polled at 1–10 Hz, GNSS at 10 Hz and the IMU at 100 Hz, all timestamped against one clock.
Pre-processing: images are corrected and resized; the IR exposure adapts to the cabin lighting.
Perception: forward perception and driver monitoring run in parallel and publish object, lane, sign and driver-state messages.
Interpretation: tracking computes TTC and headway; the drowsiness estimator updates the driver's score; vehicle and context data are refreshed.
Decision: the risk engine evaluates all inputs 10–30 times per second and decides whether to raise, escalate or clear an alert.
Response: the HMI manager plays the appropriate LED pattern, tone and voice message, and then watches for the driver's reaction.
Recording: every alert or harsh event triggers an encrypted clip from 10 seconds before to 10 seconds after.
Reporting: event data and trip statistics are uploaded over 4G (or depot Wi-Fi for clips) to the fleet dashboard and to the training pipeline, subject to consent.

Scalability is built into the design. A sensor abstraction layer lets new sensors be added without rewriting perception code, and the module-and-message architecture means new features, such as blind-spot warning, are added as new modules subscribing to existing data. On the cloud side, telemetry brokers and processing services scale horizontally as the fleet grows, and every deployed device feeds a data flywheel: hard cases found in the field are labelled and used to retrain models, which are then pushed back by OTA update. Longer term, the platform can integrate vehicle-to-everything (C-V2X) messages, an on-device conversational assistant, and, through OEM partnerships, the vehicle control needed for automatic emergency braking and lane keeping, following the fusion framework set out in Week 2.

Saarthi Copilot v1 turns the strategy of Week 1 and the feasibility findings of Week 2 into a concrete, buildable design. Two cameras, an edge AI processor and a read-only vehicle connection, organised into eleven clearly defined software modules, deliver drowsiness and distraction monitoring, collision and headway warnings, lane and road-edge departure warnings, overspeed alerts and vehicle health insights, all within a 90 ms response budget and an affordable bill of materials. Each AI algorithm was chosen for real-time performance, accuracy on Indian data and explainability, and the hybrid decision engine adapts its warnings to the driver's state. The design is honest about its limits, particularly monocular distance accuracy and the lack of vehicle control, and it is built to scale: by adding radar, more cameras and, eventually, vehicle control, the same architecture can grow from a warning device into a full advanced driver assistance system.
